# World in Brief: Nvidia’s post-Huang earnings beat expectations; more tech disruptions

Photograph: Getty Images

Nov 17th 2026(updated 2h ago)

**Nvidia** reported bumper third-quarter earnings, beating expectations: revenues surged by 103% year on year, to $115.8bn. Nvidia’s share price rose during after-hours trading, although investors remain jittery about the chipmaker’s future following the ouster of its boss, **Jensen Huang**, over his affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The company’s market capitalisation has shrunk by around $500bn since his departure last week; America’s tech-heavy NASDAQ closed 0.7% lower on Tuesday. Earlier, Mr Huang said he would be “honoured” to return to Nvidia.

cross_market_chains.chain_title: 主线一：Anthropic巨型IPO破冰与企业“去中层化”引发的AI估值锚切换

cross_market_chains.macro_channel: 一级市场流动性极限倒逼AI独角兽转向二级市场完成百亿美元级CapEx融资闭环；企业资本开支从“盲目囤积训练算力”转向“可量化替代白领与研发人力的B端Agent推理ROI”，提升大型企业SG&A利润率并激活全球科技ECM融资周期。
cross_market_chains.us_mapping: 利好Anthropic核心云股东与定制ASIC芯片（AMZN, GOOGL, AVGO）、企业级工作流与HCM软件（NOW, WDAY）及华尔街投行（GS, MS）；剧烈挤压传统IT外包与低壁垒按席位计费SaaS（EPAM, RHI）。
cross_market_chains.cn_mapping: 强力提振北美推理算力光模块与AI服务器供应链（中际旭创、新易盛、工业富联），重估国产B端编程/办公智能体与私有化算力底座（金山办公、科大讯飞、寒武纪），并催化港股科技与科创板创投估值（香港交易所）。

cross_market_chains.chain_title: 主线二：美国民生通胀反噬、执政党败选与消费供应链的“利润率大迁徙”

cross_market_chains.macro_channel: 关税传导与能源溢价令企业投入成本刚性化，而终端消费者价格弹性陡增叠加两党打击高物价的监管压力，迫使美股零售商削减毛利率并通过供应链自动化与高性价比海外采购来维持自由现金流。
cross_market_chains.us_mapping: 资金涌入具备极强议价权与规模护城河的仓储会员店及折扣店（COST, WMT, TJX）以及仓储物流自动化技术商（SYM）；抛售利润率受双面夹击的蛋白加工、包装食品与中端餐饮（TSN, KHC, SBUX）。
cross_market_chains.cn_mapping: 反向利好中国具备全球成本统治力的出海制造、智能仓储物流设备、家电ODM及跨境电商平台（拼多多 PDD、美的集团、石头科技、杭叉集团），承接欧美消费者降级与零售商控本的刚性订单。
cross_market_chains.divergence_insight: 美股消费板块交易的是“定价权丧失后的内生利润率保卫战”，估值溢价高度集中于少数渠道寡头；中国制造业则交易“供应链极致效率的全球份额变现”，但需通过海外本土化产能布局规避潜在的贸易摩擦反复。

The party’s new leaders pledged to end an unpopular war in the Middle East, lower prices and restore the American Dream. Mr Obama was not there, but his influence was hard to miss.

core_articles.title: Asia Bulletin newsletter: Xi, Trump, Putin and a theme park
core_articles.description: Jeremy Page, Chief China correspondent, on why Shenzhen is China’s window on the world
core_articles.lead_excerpt:
M y first full-time job was in Shenzhen. I moved to the city in southern China in 1997, shortly after British rule ended in neighbouring Hong Kong. In those days Shenzhen was a messy place, full of construction sites, dodgy karaoke bars and markets peddling pirated goods. It had come a long way since 1980, when a cluster of fishing villages and market towns in the area was designated as a “special economic zone” to attract foreign investment. There were only about 300,000 residents at first. By the time I arrived, there were 5m, from all over China. But it still lagged far behind Hong Kong in its infrastructure and living standards.

One of Shenzhen’s main attractions then was a theme park called Window of the World. It had replicas of the world’s top tourist sites, including a 108-metre-high copy of the Eiffel Tower. I used to go there with friends, often with a handful of beers. We’d share one on top of the ersatz Parisian monument, another at the Taj Mahal, one more at Niagara Falls. And so on. For my Chinese friends, who could not afford overseas travel then, it was the closest they could get to seeing such places for real. And it was a lot more fun than the nearby China Folk Cultural Village, which was heavy on propaganda about Chinese ethnic minorities.

I’ll be back reporting in Shenzhen this week for an updated impression of how China sees the world—and vice versa. Xi Jinping, China’s leader, is hosting a conference of Asia-Pacific powers in the city on November 18th and 19th. More importantly, on the second day, there will be a rare trilateral meeting between Mr Xi, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. The trio are not expected to reach any substantial agreements. Instead, Mr Xi will use the occasion to promote his vision of a new China-centred world order, which he likes to call “a community with a shared future for mankind”.

It is also a chance to show off Shenzhen’s extraordinary development. Today, it is a metropolis of 18m people where you can get your coffee delivered by drone, hire a robot to clean your apartment and pay for groceries by swiping your palm. It is home to the world’s biggest producers of electrical vehicles (BYD), telecommunications equipment (Huawei), aerial drones (DJI) and 3 D printers (Bambu Lab). And though still cheaper than Hong Kong, its infrastructure and living standards compare so favourably that many residents of the former British enclave visit regularly for shopping, food and medical care.
